en.title: CSIRO's sBeacon: Serverless Genomic Queries and Operational Limits on AWS
en.summary: CSIRO's sBeacon uses Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon Athena and Amazon DynamoDB to query genomic data while leaving the genomic files in their original storage. In CSIRO's chromosome 1 benchmark with 2504 individuals, sBeacon onboarded a 1.1 GB compressed VCF dataset in 18 seconds. AWS reports that whole-genome range queries time out at API Gateway, and throttled Lambda calls can lose results on HTTP 429 unless the application handles them.

claims.text: CSIRO's sBeacon uses Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon Athena and Amazon DynamoDB to query genomic data while leaving the genomic files in their original storage.

evidence.quote: sBeacon is a production-ready implementation of this standard, built using AWS services: Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) , AWS Lambda , Amazon DynamoDB , and Amazon Athena .
Note that genomic data is not copied out of its original location but rather is referenced when needed.

claims.text: In CSIRO's chromosome 1 benchmark with 2504 individuals, sBeacon onboarded a 1.1 GB compressed VCF dataset in 18 seconds.

evidence.quote: This multi-sample VCF is approximately 1.1 GB compressed, with data stored in Amazon S3.
sBeacon can ingest chromosome 1 from the 2504 individuals in 18 seconds, for less than 1 cent (USD 0.00052).

claims.text: AWS reports that whole-genome range queries time out at API Gateway, and throttled Lambda calls can lose results on HTTP 429 unless the application handles them.

evidence.quote: However, if you accidentally attempt to run a range query of the entire genome, the architecture times out at the Amazon API Gateway level.

Similarly, because synchronous Lambda invoke does not automatically retry on throttle, a 429 response from a performQuery invocation means the result is silently lost unless the application handles it explicitly.
